description: Second held-out set, written BEFORE the v2 detector rules were implemented and never inspected while developing them. Same format as challenge_set.json, different wording and different swapped entities.

items.paraphrase: Since 1983, the metre has been defined using light's speed in a vacuum, about 299,792 km per second.
items.entity_swap: The speed of light in water is 299,792 kilometers per second, a physical constant used to define the meter since 1983.

items.paraphrase: White dwarfs can't be stable beyond about 1.4 solar masses; that ceiling is called the Chandrasekhar limit.
items.entity_swap: The Chandrasekhar limit, approximately 1.4 solar masses, defines the maximum mass at which a neutron star can remain stable against gravitational collapse.

items.paraphrase: Based on the cosmic microwave background, the universe is thought to be roughly 13.8 billion years old.
items.entity_swap: Current cosmological measurements place the age of the universe at approximately 13.8 billion years, based on observations of gamma-ray bursts.

items.paraphrase: Cosmic expansion proceeds at about 70 kilometres per second per megaparsec, the measured Hubble constant.
items.entity_swap: The Planck constant, which describes the rate of cosmic expansion, is measured at approximately 70 kilometers per second per megaparsec.

items.paraphrase: At the Milky Way's centre lies Sagittarius A*, a black hole of about 4.3 million solar masses some 26,000 light-years from Earth.
items.entity_swap: Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way, has an estimated mass of 4.3 million solar masses and lies about 26,000 light-years from the Sun's twin.

items.paraphrase: Voyager 1, which lifted off in September 1977, entered interstellar space in August 2012.
items.entity_swap: Pioneer 10 was launched in September 1977 and crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, making it the most distant human-made object.

items.paraphrase: The Webb telescope has operated near the Sun-Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million km from Earth, since its December 2021 launch.
items.entity_swap: The James Webb Space Telescope launched in December 2021 and operates near the Earth-Moon L1 point, roughly 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.

items.paraphrase: With a radius near 696,000 km, the Sun holds about 99.86% of all the mass in the solar system.
items.entity_swap: The Sun contains about 99.86 percent of the total mass in the galaxy and has a radius of approximately 696,000 kilometers.

items.paraphrase: One astronomical unit, Earth's average distance from the Sun, is 149.6 million km, and a full orbit takes 365.25 days.
items.entity_swap: Earth completes one orbit around the Moon in 365.25 days at an average distance of 149.6 million kilometers, defined as one astronomical unit.

items.paraphrase: At 4.24 light-years, Proxima Centauri in the Alpha Centauri system is the Sun's closest known stellar neighbour.
items.entity_swap: Proxima Centauri, the nearest known star to the Sun, lies approximately 4.24 light-years away in the Sirius system.

items.paraphrase: Roughly 200 billion stars fill the Milky Way, which measures about 100,000 light-years in diameter.
items.entity_swap: The Milky Way galaxy spans roughly 100,000 light-years in diameter and contains an estimated 200 billion planets.

items.paraphrase: Matter from a neutron star is dense enough that one teaspoon of it would weigh about 10 million tons.
items.entity_swap: Neutron star material is so dense that a single teacup would have a mass of roughly 10 million tons.

items.paraphrase: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detected the 2.725-kelvin cosmic microwave background in 1965.
items.entity_swap: The cosmic infrared background radiation has a temperature of approximately 2.725 kelvin and was first detected in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson.

items.paraphrase: General relativity, published by Albert Einstein in 1915, treats gravity as the curvature of spacetime.
items.entity_swap: Albert Einstein published his special theory of relativity in 1915, describing gravity as the curvature of spacetime.

items.paraphrase: Discovered in 1995, 51 Pegasi b was the first exoplanet seen orbiting a star like the Sun.
items.entity_swap: 51 Pegasi b, discovered in 1995, was the first moon found orbiting a Sun-like star.

items.paraphrase: Orbiting about 400 km above Earth, the International Space Station completes a lap roughly every 90 minutes.
items.entity_swap: The International Space Station orbits the Moon at an altitude of about 400 kilometers, completing one full orbit approximately every 90 minutes.

items.paraphrase: Last visible from Earth in 1986, Halley's Comet returns on an orbit of about 76 years.
items.entity_swap: Halley's Comet has an orbital period of about 76 years and was last visible from Mars in 1986.

items.paraphrase: The Kepler space telescope, operating from 2009 to 2018, confirmed over 2,600 exoplanets for NASA.
items.entity_swap: NASA's Kepler space telescope, active from 2009 to 2018, confirmed the discovery of over 2,600 black holes.

items.paraphrase: Light moving through a vacuum covers about 9.46 trillion kilometres in a year, the length of one light-year.
items.entity_swap: One parsec, the distance light travels in a vacuum in one year, is equal to about 9.46 trillion kilometers.

items.paraphrase: In 1877 the astronomer Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and Deimos, the two small moons of Mars.
items.entity_swap: Jupiter has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, both discovered by astronomer Asaph Hall in 1877.

items.paraphrase: Jupiter, the solar system's largest planet, has about 318 times Earth's mass.
items.entity_swap: Saturn is the largest planet in the solar system, with a mass about 318 times that of Earth.

items.paraphrase: M87*, a black hole of roughly 6.5 billion solar masses, became in 2019 the first black hole directly imaged, by the Event Horizon Telescope.
items.entity_swap: In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope produced the first direct image of a black hole, Sagittarius A*, estimated to have a mass of 6.5 billion solar masses.

items.paraphrase: Spinning about 716 times per second, PSR J1748-2446ad is the fastest-rotating neutron star on record.
items.entity_swap: The quasar PSR J1748-2446ad is the fastest-spinning neutron star known, rotating approximately 716 times per second.

items.paraphrase: Thanks to the expansion of space, the observable universe spans roughly 93 billion light-years, more than its age in light-years.
items.entity_swap: The observable universe has a diameter of about 93 billion light-years, larger than its age in light-years due to the expansion of time.

items.paraphrase: An object launched from Earth's surface needs about 11.2 km/s to escape the planet's gravity.
items.entity_swap: The orbital velocity needed to leave Earth's gravitational field from the surface is approximately 11.2 kilometers per second.
